subject: computing
title: Recursion: factorial(4) — the Call Stack Grows, Then Unwinds
objectives: Trace the calls in order: factorial(4) calls factorial(3), factorial(3) calls factorial(2), factorial(2) calls factorial(1)
Explain why the base case stops the descent and why the stack unwinds in reverse order
State the value each frame returns on the unwind, ending with factorial(4) returning 24

definitions.meaning: A function solving a problem by calling itself on a smaller input; in this animation factorial calls itself with n - 1 until the base case stops the descent.
The smallest input that is answered directly without a further recursive call; here factorial(1) is the base case and it returns 1.
The stack of suspended calls, first call at the bottom; it grows as the calls descend and shrinks as the frames return on the unwind.
One suspended call held on the call stack, keeping its place and its pending multiplication while it waits for the call above it to return.
The value a call hands back to its caller; the base case returns 1, and each resumed frame returns its product, ending with 24 from factorial(4).
A call a function makes to itself on a smaller input; each recursive call pauses its caller and stacks a new frame while the caller waits.
The return journey of the recursion: once the base case returns, the frames resume in reverse order, each multiplying and passing its product back down.

mechanismSteps: The calls descend: factorial(4) pauses and calls factorial(3), which pauses and calls factorial(2), stacking a new frame for each call while every caller waits (s1).
Down to the base case: factorial(2) pauses and calls factorial(1), which calls nothing and returns 1 at once, so the descent stops (s2).
The stack unwinds: factorial(2) resumes and returns 2, then factorial(3) resumes and returns 6, the frames completing in reverse order (s3).
The outermost frame returns the answer: factorial(4) resumes last, returns 4 x 6 = 24, and the call stack is empty (s4).
workedExample: Trace factorial(4) frame by frame. Step 1 (s1): factorial(4) pauses and calls factorial(3); factorial(3) pauses and calls factorial(2); factorial(2) pauses and calls factorial(1), so four frames sit on the call stack. Step 2 (s2): factorial(1) is the base case - it calls nothing and the base case returns 1, so the descent stops. Step 3 (s3): the stack unwinds in reverse order - factorial(2) resumes and returns 2 x 1 = 2 and factorial(3) resumes and returns 3 x 2 = 6, so the running products are 1, 2, 6, 24 in the making. Step 4 (s4): factorial(4) resumes last and returns 4 x 6 = 24 - the outermost frame returns the answer and the stack is empty.

trap.misconception: A recursive call replaces the caller, so factorial(4) is finished and gone once factorial(3) starts.
trap.explanation: The slip: The caller visibly pauses and the new call takes over the screen, so it reads as a replacement - the suspended caller is out of sight while the callee runs, and nothing seems to remain of it. The fix: The caller is not replaced: it is suspended on the call stack, still holding its place and its pending multiplication, and it resumes exactly where it stopped when the callee returns - which is why the stack unwinds in reverse order, multiplying 1, 2, 6, 24. In class, replay scene 1: freeze while factorial(3) is running and ask where factorial(4) is at that moment - suspended on the call stack with its multiplication still pending - which is why it can resume and multiply when factorial(3) returns.
